summary:
We built a single, install-free browser application that joins two linked experiences. The first is a first-person Mars EVA field simulator rendered in WebGL: the astronaut walks, lopes and jumps across procedurally generated terrain modelled on Jezero Crater, Olympus Mons, Valles Marineris, Hellas Basin and Gale Crater, under a physically honest Mars — 3.71 m/s² gravity, a 142 kg suited mass, a 768 Pa CO₂ atmosphere, traction-limited gait, slope sliding past 31°, ballistic regolith instead of billowing dust, dust devils, and a full 24h 39m sol cycle with live suit telemetry for oxygen, heater power, suit integrity and radiation dose.

From the suit’s wrist display, the astronaut opens the second experience: an interactive 2D/3D Mars atlas built on NASA MGS-MOLA MEGDR elevation and USGS planetary geologic units. It layers hazard mapping (slope, radiation, dunes and storms, seismicity), eleven NASA landmarks with Photojournal imagery, Curiosity’s seven-stop Mount Sharp route, and a base-planning tool that scores habitats, MOXIE, solar arrays and rovers on distance synergy, terrain, solar and oxygen availability, and hazard safety.

It matters because it turns scattered mission datasets into an embodied, intuitive tool for site-selection reasoning and risk literacy — available in English, Turkish and French to anyone with a browser.
details:
What it does and how it works

The project is a single self-contained HTML application that runs in any modern browser with no installation, no server and no account. It contains two tightly coupled experiences that share one simulated Mars.

The first is a first-person EVA field simulator. The player is a suited astronaut standing on procedurally generated Martian terrain. The surface is built from layered value-noise and fBm functions, then shaped by real landform geometry: six craters with rims, floors and central peaks, Mount Sharp as a central mound inside Gale, a swept canyon profile for Valles Marineris, dune fields, scattered collidable boulders, and a deterministic pebble field that regenerates per grid cell as the player moves, so detail is infinite without ever being stored.

Movement is not animation — it is integrated physics. Gravity is 3.71 m/s², the astronaut plus EVA suit masses 142 kg, and the gait is traction-limited: friction can only change velocity by μN/m per second, so with μ = 0.60 on regolith and 0.85 on rock, starts and stops take visibly long and turns overshoot. Slopes always apply a tangential gravity component, and past roughly 31° the astronaut begins to slide. Jumps and thrown rocks fly as true ballistic arcs with CO₂ drag computed relative to the wind, using a 0.9 m² drag area for the suited body. Because the atmosphere is 768 Pa, drag is almost negligible, so kicked-up regolith travels in clean parabolas rather than billowing — a detail that reads instantly as “not Earth.” Wind exerts only a fraction of a newton on 142 kg, and the HUD shows that honestly. A fixed sub-step integrator keeps the simulation stable even at low frame rates.

Around the player we modelled the environment rather than decorating it. A full sol runs 88,775 seconds and can be scaled ×1, ×60 or ×600; the sky dome shifts from butterscotch daylight through grey twilight to a near-black night, with the characteristic blue glow around a low sun, and sunlight colour and intensity track solar elevation. Atmospheric density is derived from the ideal gas law for CO₂ at the current temperature, which in turn feeds air density, the speed of sound (around 226 m/s), terminal velocity and wind force. Ambient dust motes, ballistic regolith puffs and dust devils are all separate particle systems driven by the same environment state.

The suit is a resource system. Oxygen, heater battery and suit integrity drain over the EVA; heater draw rises as temperature falls; accumulated radiation dose is tracked in µSv against a live µSv/h rate; and the status readout degrades from nominal as the weakest subsystem drops. Pressing F takes a regolith sample and fills a tube, which is logged in an inventory panel.

The second experience is the atlas, opened from the astronaut’s own left-arm holographic terminal. When the player raises the wrist display and presses M, the field simulation pauses and the full interactive Mars atlas loads inside the visor. The atlas is a complete second application, embedded in the same file as base64 and decoded into a sandboxed frame at runtime, with its keyboard events bridged back to the parent so the two never fight over input.

The atlas itself is a planning and analysis tool. It presents Mars in both 2D map and 3D globe form, with auto-rotation, MOLA relief, a night terminator and a coordinate grid. Elevation comes from NASA MGS-MOLA MEGDR data, classified across seven bands from below −4,000 m to above +14,000 m, with a graceful fallback to a verified built-in MOLA dataset when the remote service is unreachable. On top of this sit a hazard map with a traffic-light classification (safe below 8°, moderate 8–18°, critical above 18° or under radiation and storm risk) and selectable sub-layers for slope and cliffs, radiation, dunes and storms, and seismicity and rockfall.

Eleven real sites — Jezero, Olympus Mons, Valles Marineris, Gale, Hellas, Noctis Labyrinthus, Victoria and Endurance, Viking 1 and 2, InSight and Planum Boreum — each open a five-tab dossier: terrain type and USGS geologic unit, hazard breakdown, environment (temperature range, pressure, wind and dust-storm risk, radiation and insolation), the sol cycle with CO₂ shielding mass, and base viability, including rover and EVA traversability at 0.38 G and estimated suit endurance. Curiosity’s seven-stop Lower Mount Sharp ascent is included as a playable route animation from the Gale floor into the sulphate and Gediz Vallis layers.

Finally, the atlas is a base designer. Users place habitats, MOXIE oxygen plants, solar arrays, rovers, EVA astronauts, routes, hazard zones and notes directly on the map, and each structure is scored out of 100 across four weighted dimensions: inter-structure distance synergy (35), MOLA elevation and slope (25), solar, oxygen and atmospheric conditions (25), and hazard safety (15), with a full-screen report explaining every gain and penalty. A habitat and life-support panel aggregates power and oxygen balance across everything placed.

Benefits and intended impact

The data our project rests on is public, excellent and almost completely inaccessible to non-specialists. MOLA elevation grids, USGS geologic unit codes and mission traverse data are distributed as raster products and technical papers; reading them requires GIS skills and domain vocabulary. Our intent was to make that same data answer a human question — could a person live and work here, and what would it feel like?

The two halves do different work toward that. The atlas builds analytical literacy: why a delta floor at −2,540 m with 4.2° slopes is a defensible landing site and a 21,229 m volcanic summit is not, why structure spacing matters, why hazard classes are not interchangeable. The field simulator builds intuition that no chart conveys: that low gravity makes you slow to stop rather than nimble, that thin air means dust falls instead of hanging, that a slope you could walk up on Earth will slide you down here, that oxygen and heater power are a clock you are always running against.

We see the clearest impact in education and outreach — classrooms, planetariums, science centres and public engagement around Mars missions — and as an accessible first-pass site-selection and risk-reasoning tool for students, hackathon teams and space-interest communities. The interface ships in English, Turkish and French, which matters for reaching audiences that most planetary science software never addresses.

Tools and technologies

The entire project is one HTML file built with vanilla JavaScript, HTML5 and CSS — no build step, no framework, no backend. 3D rendering uses Three.js (r128) with WebGL, including a procedurally generated regolith grain texture drawn to canvas at runtime, custom sky-dome shading, point-sprite particle systems and dynamic shadow casting from an invisible body proxy. Tailwind CSS handles the HUD and atlas interface, with Font Awesome icons and the Inter and JetBrains Mono typefaces. The Pointer Lock API provides mouse-look. The atlas is embedded via base64 encoding and injected as iframe srcdoc, decoded with TextDecoder. All physics, terrain generation, noise functions, atmospheric modelling and scoring logic are hand-written. It needs only a browser — no hardware, no GPU beyond standard WebGL support, no network connection after first load.

Creativity

The creative core of the project is the wrist terminal. Rather than presenting a simulator and a data dashboard as two separate products, we made the dashboard a diegetic object inside the simulation: the astronaut raises their own arm, a hologram lights up, and the planetary atlas opens in their visor. Scale collapses in one gesture — from the half-metre of regolith at your boots to the whole planet and back — and the data stops being a reference you consult and becomes equipment you carry.

We also chose accuracy as an aesthetic strategy. The most memorable moments in the simulator come from refusing to exaggerate: regolith that arcs instead of clouding, a 0.5 N wind force printed next to a 527 N body weight, a dust devil that is eerie precisely because it is quiet. And embedding a complete second application inside a single file, decoded at runtime, let us ship a genuinely two-part experience under the constraint of one shareable HTML document.

Factors we considered

Scientific fidelity came first: every constant in the simulation is a published value, and where the real figure is undramatic we showed the real figure. Accessibility came next — zero install, zero cost, one file, works offline, three languages, and a graceful data fallback so the tool never breaks in a classroom with poor connectivity. Performance mattered because reach depends on it, so terrain detail is procedural and player-local rather than preloaded, and the integrator is sub-stepped to stay correct on weak hardware. We considered pedagogy in the pairing itself: embodied experience alone produces wonder without understanding, and data alone produces understanding without motivation, so the design deliberately requires both. And we kept the whole thing honest about uncertainty — hazard classes are presented as risk bands, data sources are listed and verifiable, and the built-in dataset announces itself when the live service cannot be reached.
